children: HEADLINES
BMO, Sun Life Pledge C$75 Billion Private Capital for Infrastructure Push
Bank of Montreal and Sun Life Financial have committed to bankroll Ottawa's economic security agenda, pledging C$75 billion in private-sector capital to support Canada's infrastructure push.

Two of Canada's largest financial institutions made the announcements Friday, with BMO planning to mobilize up to C$70 billion over the next decade through commercial capital for sectors critical to Canadian economic security and resilience, including power generation, oil and gas pipelines, transportation infrastructure and artificial intelligence computing, among others.
At the same time, institutional asset manager Sun Life launched its own C$5 billion initiative to take direct debt and equity stakes in major national projects.
Canada to Pursue Legislation to Revamp Regulatory System
Canada's Liberal government will introduce legislation in the coming weeks that builds upon previous efforts to accelerate the construction of projects and attract private capital.

Senior cabinet minister Dominic LeBlanc said the proposed changes to project reviews will maintain robust environmental protection and respect Ottawa's constitutional responsibility to consult with the country's indigenous communities.

Besides managing a turbulent trade relationship with the U.S., Prime Minister Mark Carney has made the lure of private investment and the construction of infrastructure and resource projects an urgent policy priority. Some of his most notable policy changes to date have focused on establishing more certainty regarding the regulatory-review process.
Stellantis Talks With Canadian Workers Hit Impasse on Plan to Sell Ontario Factory, Union Says

Stellantis is in talks to sell its idled Toronto-area factory to a local defense firm, prompting the union representing over 9,000 of the automaker's Canadian employees to declare an impasse on talks toward a new labor deal.
The potential sale is the latest development involving the Stellantis factory in Brampton, Ontario, which hasn't operated since 2024 to undergo retooling.

Stellantis last year unveiled plans to shift the production of its next-generation Jeep Compass to Illinois from Brampton amid hefty Trump administration tariffs on foreign-made cars. The decision sparked the threat of a lawsuit from the Canadian government, which had provided Stellantis with hundreds of millions for work at the plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ontario.
Descartes Systems Group Posts Quarterly Beat, AI Strategy Update
Descartes Systems Group reported better-than-expected results in its second quarter, and outlined its artificial intelligence strategy.
Shares jumped 6.9% to settle at C$105.32.

The logistics software company reported a 12% rise in revenue to $201.1 million, surpassing the $200.5 million expected by analysts. A large portion of the growth was from services and other revenue, which reached $188.6 million, and makes up 94% of total revenue.
Net income surged to $50 million for the three months ended July 31, compared with $38 million a year earlier, which on a per-share basis was 57 cents compared with 43 cents.
Roots Loss Widens, Sales Slip
Roots logged a widened loss in its second quarter as sales fell.

The Canadian outdoor lifestyle brand reported a widened loss of C$6 million, or C$0.15 a share in the three months ended Aug. 1, compared with a loss of C$4.4 million, or C$0.11 a share a year earlier.
Adjusted loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization narrowed to C$1.6 million from a loss of C$2.1 million.
Sales fell 2.4% to C$49.5 million, with direct-to-consumer sales slipping 1.3% from a year earlier. Direct-to-consumer comparable sales also fell, down 1%.
Celestica Appoints Todd Ankenmann as Finance Chief
Celestica has appointed Todd Ankenmann as its new chief financial officer, effective at the start of October.

Ankenmann succeeds long-time CFO Mandeep Chawla in the role. Chawla, who has been with Celestica since 2010 and the last nine years as chief of finance, has been appointed Group President, Global Markets with a mandate to oversee Celestica's overarching commercial execution and global market expansion.

Ankenmann has been with the electronics manufacturing services company since 2018, and currently serves as its senior vice president of finance. Before that, he spent over a decade in senior finance leadership roles at General Electric.
Household Net Worth Rose on Stock-Market Gains

Household net worth in Canada rose in the second quarter, and the stock of credit-market debt as a share of after-tax household income recorded its biggest drop in nearly two years, Statistics Canada said.

The net worth of Canadian households rose 2.9% on an unadjusted basis in the second quarter to surpass the threshold of C$19 trillion, powered by gains in the equity markets. Household liabilities, mostly mortgages and nonmortgage debt, climbed 1.3%

The closely watched ratio of credit-market debt to after-tax income rose slightly on an unadjusted basis in the April-to-June period, to 175.06%. The data agency noted, however, that on a seasonally adjusted basis, that ratio declined to 176.4% from 178.6%, marking the largest drop since the third quarter of 2024. Income grew at over twice the pace of debt in that period, Statistics Canada said.
Embattled Sen. Susan Collins Criticizes Trump's Canada Insults

Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who faces her toughest re-election campaign to date, is working closely with top Trump administration officials to try to lessen the impact of the U.S.'s escalating trade dispute with Canada.

But she says President Trump's own tone and rhetoric surrounding the tariffs have been inappropriate and unhelpful in her border state, whose culture and economy is intertwined with the U.S.'s northern neighbor.

"We're linked in so many ways. It's economic, it's emotional, and to hear the president gratuitously calling prime ministers 'governor' or suggesting that Canada should be part of the United States or renaming Lake Ontario is painful," Collins said in an interview. "It is not conducive to getting back to the table and resolving these issues."
JPMorgan: Eight of Nine Developed-Market Central Banks to Lift Rates Soon

JPMorgan Chase analysts expect eight of the world's nine developed-market central banks to lift interest rates before the end of the year in efforts to tame sticky inflation and commodity price pressures.

The analysts said they expect rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, as well as from central banks in Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Norway and Sweden.
They forecast the Bank of Canada to be "the lonesome dove."
JPMorgan said its base case was for the Fed to hold rates next week and lift them in December. The ECB raised rates Thursday, and JPMorgan expects a further hike before year end.
TALKING POINT
Canada Pins Hope for Economic Turbocharge on High-Profile Investor Summit
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Deep-pocketed global investors descend on Toronto early next week at the invitation of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is banking on their cash to help shift his restructuring of the country's economy into a higher gear.

Starting Monday, Carney hosts an investment summit that officials have likened to a matchmaking exercise, pairing companies pitching projects with some of the world's top asset managers responsible for assets totaling over $100 trillion. Wall Street heavyweights alongside sovereign-wealth and pension funds will size up over two days pitches for over 160 projects from Canadian executives in fields covering conventional and clean energy, mining, defense manufacturing, and power generation, according to a prospectus prepared for invitees and reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The gathering marks a high-profile push by Carney to rewire an economy that was struggling prior to the start of President Trump's second term, and which has been trying to navigate under the weight of hefty U.S. tariffs on key sectors and elevated uncertainty over preferential access to the world's biggest economy. Carney seeks to attract 1 trillion Canadian dollars (US$723 billion) over the next five years to build up economic resilience, and reshape a country that became too reliant and complacent on U.S. trade to drive growth.

Investors attending "are coming because of Canada. If they wanted to go to the United States, they go to the United States," Carney said. "What they are going to see when they come here is a country that is uniting, that is positive...and a country that respects rule of law and that is reliable--and that combination is pretty rare in the world."

Among the Canadian firms keen on cash at the summit is Deep Sky, a Montreal-based company that develops carbon-removal projects. The company is looking for $328 million from strategic investors to build its biggest carbon-capture and sequestration facility to date in oil-rich Alberta. Through its other facility, also in Alberta, Deep Sky has been able to sell carbon credits to Microsoft and other leading financing institutions, said Quentin Servais-Laval, the company's vice-president of finance.

The summit "will help put infrastructure projects that are shovel-ready in front of investors that have the funds to deploy and are really interested in the opportunity in Canada," Servais-Laval said, adding the company has meetings lined up in Toronto regarding its proposed plant. "So for me, it's an accelerator." The summit comes at a crucial period for the Canadian economy, which recently showed signs of a breakthrough after 12 months of stagnant activity stemming from trade uncertainty. Economic ties between Canada and the U.S. have deteriorated in the past three weeks after talks toward a tariff deal collapsed, prompting both countries to impose new tariffs and restrictions on cross-border trade. On an individual-country basis, Canada is America's second-largest trading partner, with two-way annual trade of roughly $1 trillion.

A report published by Royal Bank of Canada said, based on analysis of United Nations data, Canada has attracted nearly 4% of global-inward foreign-direct investment, an admirable share for an economy that accounts for 2% of global output. "But relative to its potential--abundant resources, a highly educated workforce, and clean, affordable power--Canada remains an underinvested jurisdiction," the report said.

Part of the problem is weak domestic investment, which analysts say is partly thwarted by structural flaws. Top of the list, Royal Bank said, is an opaque and shifting regulatory system that extends times and increases capital costs. Royal Bank noted that, for instance, Canadian mining projects average over 20 years from discovery to production, versus over 13 years in Australia. The report added that regulatory delays and uncertainty contributed to the cancellations of eight proposed liquefied-natural-gas projects.

The Carney government has moved to reduce regulatory overlap and accelerate project approval. It made a key change this week by scaling back project assessments required for oil-and-gas pipelines and natural-gas plants.
